title: IOC clears FIFA president Gianni Infantino of breaching political neutrality rules
content:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino has been cleared by the International Olympic Committee of breaching its rules on political neutrality.

Infantino, who is an IOC member, appeared alongside United States president Donald Trump on Thursday at the inaugural Board of Peace meeting, where the focus was on reconstruction plans in Gaza once the conflict ends.

Kirsty Coventry, the IOC president, was questioned about Infantino’s appearance at the event on Thursday during a press conference at the Winter Olympics. The 55-year-old had worn a red ‘USA’ cap, with the numbers ‘45-47’ on the side — a reference to Trump’s non-consecutive presidencies.

Coventry was initially unaware of the FIFA president’s attendance, but said it is something the IOC will investigate to ascertain whether its rules on political neutrality have been breached. The Olympic organization’s charter states that members must act independently of political and commercial interests, and cannot accept “from governments, organisations, or other parties, any mandate or instructions liable to interfere with the freedom of their action and vote”.

“The IOC has been in contact with FIFA. We understand that FIFA is supporting, through football, a comprehensive sport recovery investment programme in Gaza, Palestine, by providing sporting infrastructure, education and elite development proposals,” an IOC spokesperson said in a statement released to The Athletic.

“This is entirely in keeping with the role of an International Sport Federation.

“The IOC, through Olympic Solidarity, which is our development vehicle, has been and continues to support sport development in the region.”

FIFA announced a formal partnership with Trump’s Board of Peace during the event, committing to a three-stage plan to support the regeneration of Gaza. The world football governing body said the plan would include the construction of a 20,000-seater stadium within three years of work commencing.

Trump also said on Thursday that FIFA would raise $75 million in funding for “projects in Gaza” and said that they would get “the greatest stars in the world to go there.”

FIFA’s press release on the day did not say where the money would come from or how the money would be raised and it also did not say whether the Palestine Football Association had been consulted.

When pressed by The Athletic, FIFA sources, who remain anonymous as they were not authorized to speak on the matter, said they were collaborating with the Board of Peace and assessing from which project to start, who will be the financial contributors and the total amount. They claimed that the Board of Peace already has countries interested in investing, but said they could not disclose the countries involved at this point.
